title: Want big & healthy biceps? Try elastic curls
summary: NH demonstrates band curls with a light band anchored low on a rack as a finisher that keeps the biceps tendon healthy through full extension, which his heavy partial curls avoid. He explains the hand placement that removes grip, using them to work through elbow tendinitis, a side-on variant for the brachialis and forearm, and the accommodating resistance a band provides.
claims: Band curls with a light band tied low on a rack mainly support biceps tendon health and only secondarily hypertrophy
Use band curls as a finisher at the end of a biceps or arm day; on triceps and press days they help with elbow tendinitis
Sit the band deep in the palm between the fingers so you do not grip it, which takes the forearm out and reduces tension on the elbow
With the band, let the arm almost fully extend; he does heavy curls with a partial range because full extension under heavy load is dangerous for the tendon
Band curls are essentially junk volume and not a mass builder; they finish the biceps rather than build it
If you always curl with partial range, the arm loses the ability to go deep, and an accidental deep rep can snap something; band curls keep that range
Do three or four sets of AMRAP band curls at the end of the workout in a superset or giant set
With elbow tendinitis, work up to the painful point and gradually extend further over the reps; pops or crackling are fine, but do not force through pain
Standing side-on to the rack and curling hammer-style works the brachialis and forearm while staying easy on the tendons
Band curls do not hurt recovery or pressing performance because they focus on the muscle, so there is no excuse to skip curls
Bands give accommodating resistance: tension is highest at the top where you are strongest and drops as leverage gets harder
exercises: band deep in palm, no grip; arm nearly fully extended; squeeze
